interrogator_dossier:
# Axos Financial (AX) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 2026-09-22. Source material: five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (April 2025 through April 2026, covering fiscal Q3 2025 to fiscal Q3 2026), the company's fiscal-2026 results release of 30 July 2026, filed quarterly financial statements through the quarter ended 30 June 2026, and the screener's financial trajectory. Axos runs a June fiscal year, so "fiscal 2026" means the twelve months ended 30 June 2026.*

*A note on sourcing: the transcript package supplied to this committee stops at the April 2026 call. The fiscal fourth-quarter call of 30 July 2026 exists but was not included, and the data vendor returned the wrong year's content when asked for it. The fourth quarter is therefore covered here from the filed income statement and balance sheet and the company's own results release, not from management's commentary. Where a conclusion depends on that missing call, it is flagged.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Axos is a branchless, nationwide bank holding company — roughly $30 billion of assets, a $22.4 billion deposit base and a $25 billion loan book — with a small brokerage arm (Axos Clearing and Axos Invest) that provides custody to registered investment advisers and clearing to correspondent broker-dealers. Greg Garrabrants has run it for the whole period under review and, at the July 2025 call, for twenty-five years.

Across these five quarters the story changed in one clear way, and it is the most important thing in this dossier: **Axos stopped being a purely organic grower and became an acquirer.**

In April 2025 the narrative was entirely internal. Management talked about defending a net interest margin — the spread between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits — that had run near 4.8%, about a jumbo-mortgage and apartment-lending book that was shrinking faster than new lending could replace it, and about excess cash sitting on the balance sheet costing thirteen basis points of margin. The tone was of a company managing a headwind well.

By July 2025 the headwind had turned. Loan balances grew $856 million in the quarter, the mortgage runoff had stopped, and for the first time management said out loud that "the pace and quality of merger and acquisition opportunities have increased over the past few months and seller expectations have become more reasonable." That was the pivot signal, and it was accurate: within twelve months Axos closed the Verdant equipment-finance acquisition (30 September 2025), bought roughly $2.3 billion of deposits from Jenius Bank (converted around the end of April 2026), took on retirement-account custody business formerly served by Capital One, purchased a commercial office building in January 2026 to serve as a future headquarters, and in July 2026 signed to acquire Arc Technologies, a small-business financial-technology platform.

A second, quieter thread runs through every call: artificial intelligence as a cost lever. This is unusual in that Garrabrants frames it as an accountability commitment rather than a slogan — "for each dollar you earn, you don't spend as much on people and technology" (April 2025) — and ties it to a published, numeric constraint: personnel and professional-services expense growth will not exceed thirty cents for every dollar of revenue growth. He restated that cap under direct questioning in July 2025, October 2025 and again when the Verdant deal muddied the baseline. By April 2026 the claimed benefits had reached the income statement: "we are seeing some of the benefits from our operational efficiency initiatives and artificial intelligence on our salaries and benefits, data processing and other general and administrative expenses."

What was quietly dropped: the stablecoin and digital-asset thread. Asked directly in July 2025, Garrabrants said Axos was "focused on it and thinking through it" but declined to comment publicly. It has not resurfaced in any subsequent call in the package. Treat it as an option the company holds, not a plan it has.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loan growth of "low to mid-teens" annually | Oct 2025, Jan 2026, Apr 2026 | Net loan growth of $856M, $1.6B (incl. Verdant), $1.0B and ~$700M in consecutive quarters; loans reached ~$25.0B | **Delivered.** Consistently at or above the stated range. |
| "Best-in-class net interest margin" | Every call | Reported margin fell from 4.94% (Dec 2025) to 4.57% (Mar 2026). Organic margin, stripping out the runoff of discount accretion on the loan pool bought from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, was roughly flat | **Delivered, but the phrase now needs an asterisk every single quarter.** The reported number is falling; the underlying number is not. |
| Expense growth capped at 30% of revenue growth | Jul 2025, Oct 2025, Jan 2026 | Non-interest expense rose only $1.4M sequentially in the March 2026 quarter, to $186M, while revenue rose | **Delivered**, and this is the single most impressive piece of execution in the file. |
| Credit quality "solid," charge-offs low | Every call | Non-accrual loans as a share of total loans fell steadily: 1.26% → 0.89% → 0.79% → 0.74% → 0.61% | **Delivered.** Five consecutive quarters of improvement is not a story, it is a trend. |
| Earnings growing at a mid-to-high teens rate | Implied throughout | Diluted earnings per share: $1.94 → $2.22 → $2.15 → $2.16 across fiscal 2026, totalling $8.48 versus $7.43 the prior year, up 14.1% | **Delivered on the headline.** See below for the quality question. |
| Tax rate will fall to 26–27% from 29–30% | Jul 2025 | Fiscal-2026 effective rate came in at **24.2%** — $156.2M of tax on $646.7M of pre-tax income | **Over-delivered, and this is the finding of the dossier.** |

### The tax-rate finding

This is where the narrative is richer than the trajectory justifies, and it is not visible in any headline.

Pre-tax income across fiscal 2026 ran $149.9M, $175.5M, $165.3M and $156.0M. It **peaked in the December 2025 quarter and declined in each of the two quarters after it.** Reported earnings per share did not decline, because the tax line did the work. The effective tax rate by quarter was 25.0%, 26.8%, 24.6% and then **19.9%** in the June 2026 quarter.

Had the June quarter been taxed at the prior quarter's 24.6% rate, net income would have been roughly $117.6M and earnings per share roughly $2.04 rather than the reported $2.16. Roughly twelve cents of the quarter — and roughly twenty-six cents of the full fiscal year, measured against management's own 26–27% guidance — came from tax, not from banking.

Part of that benefit is durable: California changed how it taxes financial institutions, and management flagged the three-percentage-point improvement a full quarter before it arrived, which is to their credit. But Derrick Walsh also disclosed, in July 2025, that the tax line "benefited from the increase in our stock price from June 30, 2024 to June 30, 2025, which is one factor used to calculate our chief executive's stock-based incentive compensation." Axos shares rose roughly 30% over the fiscal year to June 2026. **That component of the tax benefit is a function of the share price, and it reverses when the share price falls.** The stock is now 13% below its August 2026 high. Anyone modelling fiscal 2027 off a 24% tax rate is extrapolating a tailwind that has already turned.

### The adjusted-earnings gap

The June 2026 quarter reported earnings per share of $2.16 on a standard accounting basis. Zacks, comparing the quarter against a $2.15 consensus, printed the figure as $2.53 — a seventeen percent gap, implying management excluded roughly thirty-seven cents a share of charges (most plausibly deal costs on Jenius and Arc, and the day-one credit provision required on acquired loans). Without the July 2026 call this committee cannot confirm the composition. What can be confirmed is the pattern: **there has been a non-recurring item to adjust around in every single quarter of this file** — a $12M gain on apartment-loan sales and a $5.6M deferred-tax write-down (June 2025), $17M of accelerated discount accretion (December 2025), a $22M legal settlement and new headquarters rental income (March 2026). Individually each is defensible. Collectively they mean the reader, not management, does the normalising.

### The free-cash-flow flag is noise

The screener shows free cash flow down 33% year over year against earnings up 14%, and a solvency score of −0.5. Both are artefacts of applying industrial-company templates to a bank. A bank's cash flow statement is dominated by deposit and loan flows; its leverage is its business model. Neither is evidence of anything here. So is the "net cash of $89 million" line: the $1.16 billion of cash on Axos's balance sheet is liquidity held against $22.4 billion of deposits, not surplus capital available to shareholders. It must not be added to a valuation.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, and unusually so.**

- **April 2025 — defensive.** The vocabulary is about damage control: "excess liquidity was a 13 basis point drag," keeping mortgage balances "flat to down $100 million per quarter versus the prior $200 million to $400 million quarterly headwind." Asked why capital was being held at the highest level a long-time shareholder had ever seen, Garrabrants conceded: "I am a conservative guy... there is a recognition that we obviously want to continue to make sure that we have a very strong balance sheet."
- **July 2025 — the turn.** "We ended fiscal 25 with positive momentum." The acquisition window is declared open. Guidance moves to "the mid to high end" of the range rather than the middle.
- **October 2025 — confident and specific.** Verdant will add "$150 million to $200 million of net new loans and operating leases per quarter." The floor-plan team will have "several hundred million dollars, let's say, by March 31, I would guess. Maybe that's a little aggressive."
- **January 2026 — peak.** "We had an outstanding quarter across a variety of growth, credit, and profitability metrics." Verdant is described as delivering ahead of plan, including a synergy Garrabrants volunteers he did not expect: "they've been enthusiastically selling deposits and that's actually been working, which I'm kind of surprised by."
- **April 2026 — confident, and notably relaxed.** Asked whether competition was compressing loan spreads, the answer is direct rather than hedged: "I feel that spreads are stable... I don't predict that we're going to have further spread compression."

Two behavioural markers deserve weight. First, Garrabrants gives falsifiable numbers — quarterly dollar ranges, a percentage expense cap, a guess he labels as possibly aggressive. Executives who intend to miss do not do this. Second, he is willing to be tart in public. On the California tax change: "nobody was actually involved with the lobbying of the California legislature to give us such a beneficence and basically pound other banks that are not located in California." On a shareholder's complaint about quarter-end loan timing: "I'm going to convey that message to everyone in the organization immediately. It will be the first time they've heard it." That is the register of a manager who does not feel cornered.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**High.** Tracked promise by promise:

| Promised | When | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Margin stays at the high end of 4.25–4.35% excluding purchased-loan accretion | Apr 2025, reaffirmed 3× | Held. Organic margin roughly flat through March 2026. |
| Apartment and jumbo-mortgage runoff has peaked | Jul 2025 | Correct. Balances flat by December 2025, up slightly by March 2026. |
| Organic loan growth at the mid-to-high end of high-single to low-teens | Jul 2025 | Exceeded. Delivered low-to-mid teens. |
| Verdant contributes $150–200M of new loans and leases per quarter | Oct 2025 | Delivered $130M in December, $200M in March. Slightly light, then on target. |
| $600–800M of loan growth in the March 2026 quarter | Jan 2026 | Delivered ~$800M excluding warehouse lending. |
| Tax rate falls to 26–27% | Jul 2025 | Beat — arrived at 24.2%. |
| Expense growth ≤30% of revenue growth | Jul 2025, held through the Verdant re-baselining | Held. |

The screener's record of beating consensus in six of seven quarters is consistent with this. There is a mild sandbagging pattern — ranges are set so the company lands at the top of them — but the guidance is specific enough that sandbagging is visible rather than concealed. **Reliability: High.** The one caveat is that the margin promise has required an "excluding purchased-loan accretion" qualifier in every quarter, and the reported margin has now fallen 37 basis points in two quarters. The qualifier is legitimate; it is also load-bearing.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**What analysts keep returning to, and what management does with it:**

- **Deposit costs if loan growth accelerates.** David Feaster (Raymond James, July 2025) asked directly. Garrabrants answered honestly rather than defensively: "if we had loan growth similar to what we had this quarter, every quarter in the next fiscal year, then I think that might put a little pressure on funding costs." He has kept growing loans at that pace. **This is the unresolved question in the file, and it has become more urgent, not less** — the Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September 2026, its first increase since 2023, and most participants expect at least one more. Axos funds roughly 85% of its deposits with interest-paying accounts; only about $3.4 billion of $22.4 billion is non-interest-bearing. A branchless bank's funding costs reprice fast.
- **Expenses.** Tim Coffey (Janney, October 2025) opened with "I'm trying to get my arms around expenses going forward" and Garrabrants interrupted with "So am I, Tim." Candid, and also an admission that the acquisition programme has made the expense base harder to model. He redirected to the 30% cap, which he has honoured — but the cap covers only personnel and professional services, roughly 70% of non-interest expense, and explicitly excludes the depreciation now running through the equipment-leasing and headquarters lines.
- **Fee income keeping pace with lending.** Asked in July 2025, Garrabrants declined to commit: "I think we can do it, but it will be a little difficult... it's not impossible, but it will not be easy." He was right to hedge. Advisory and clearing fees totalled about $60 million in fiscal 2026 against roughly $2.19 billion of total revenue — the brokerage arm is a strategic asset and a funding source, not yet an earnings engine.
- **Loan-loss provisioning versus improving credit.** Edward Hemmelgarn (Shaker Investments, April 2025) pushed on why provisions rose while loan quality improved. The answer — that the accounting standard imports external recession probabilities — is technically correct, and Garrabrants added a disclosure most managers would omit: "if Moody's says the probability of recession is greater, that's going to increase our loan loss. Now whether or not that ultimately ends up meaning anything for us, I mean, I can have my doubts." **A rate-hiking Fed and a ten-year Treasury above five percent will push those model inputs the wrong way, mechanically, regardless of how the loans perform.**
- **What analysts are not asking about.** Nobody has pressed on the tax rate as an earnings driver. Nobody has asked what happens to the stock-price-linked component of the tax benefit if the stock falls. That is where this committee's disagreement with the street sits.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🟢 **Five consecutive quarters of improving credit.** Non-accrual loans down from 1.26% to 0.61% of loans while the book grew by roughly a quarter. Specific and corroborated by the trend, not just asserted.

🟢 **A numeric expense discipline that has survived an acquisition.** The 30% cap was restated under pressure in three separate calls and re-baselined transparently for Verdant rather than quietly abandoned.

🟢 **Book value per share compounding at 17–19% year over year**, reported in every quarter and consistent with the screener's five-year 19.2% rate. For a bank this is the number that matters most, and it is the cleanest thing in the file.

🟢 **Opportunistic buybacks at genuine lows.** Roughly $31 million repurchased in April 2025 at an average of $59 a share, during a market swoon. The shares are now near $91. Management has demonstrated it buys when others cannot.

🟢 **Verdant integrated ahead of plan**, with an unforecast deposit-gathering synergy, and management said so without overclaiming.

🔴 **The June 2026 quarter's earnings growth came from the tax line while pre-tax income fell for a second consecutive quarter.** Detailed in section 2. This is the most important unflagged item in the file.

🔴 **A non-recurring item in every single quarter.** Five for five. Each is defensible; the pattern means the reported series is not clean.

🔴 **Reported net interest margin down 37 basis points in two quarters** (4.94% to 4.57%), with the "best-in-class" claim now dependent on an exclusion that must be restated every quarter as the purchased-loan accretion runs off toward five basis points.

🔴 **Funding structure is the structural soft spot.** Only about 15% of deposits are non-interest-bearing. A branch bank keeps a large share of deposits that cost nothing regardless of rates; a branchless bank does not. In a hiking cycle this is the difference between a margin that expands and one that compresses.

🔴 **No insider has bought in the open market.** The only recent transactions, dated 15 September 2026, are routine restricted-stock vestings with shares withheld for taxes at $92.68 — not open-market conviction. Across a 13% drawdown in a company whose chief executive is a large holder, the absence is worth noting, though it is an absence of a signal rather than a negative one.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

- **"We may have more variance from quarter-to-quarter" (April 2025) disappeared from the script** once growth resumed. The hedge was real and its removal was earned.
- **The competitive frame shifted from banks to non-banks.** By October 2025 Garrabrants was fielding questions about lending through non-depository financial institutions and defending it with an argument most bank chief executives would not risk making in public: that fraud is "much more likely" in small-business and direct-borrower lending than in large syndicated facilities. It is a considered position rather than a talking point, but it is also a bet that the market currently distrusts. Credit anxiety in 2026 is concentrated precisely in lending to non-bank financial firms and in private credit, where the default rate reached a record 6.3% over the twelve months to August 2026.
- **The technology language matured from aspiration to measurement.** April 2025: "I think we have to hold ourselves accountable for actually seeing that in the results." April 2026: the efficiency benefit is named in the prepared remarks as a driver of the expense line. Fifteen months from claim to evidence.
- **Two new voices appeared and both talk about fees rather than spread** — Michael Watson as head of Axos Securities and a renewed push on the "Axos Complete" adviser workstation. The strategic direction is toward fee income and non-interest-bearing operating deposits. It is directionally right and, so far, financially small.
- **A commercial office building was purchased in January 2026** as a future headquarters, large enough that the surplus space is leased out and generates roughly $4 million a quarter of rental income. A branchless bank buying an oversized office building is a mild capital-allocation oddity. It has not been challenged on a call in this file.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**STRENGTHENING.**

Axos entered this period defending a shrinking mortgage book and exited it as a $30 billion, 16% return-on-equity bank compounding tangible book value in the high teens, with credit improving for five straight quarters, an expense discipline that held through two acquisitions, and an integration record that has so far beaten its own forecasts. Management says specific, checkable things and has been right about most of them.

# Axos Financial (AX) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Debate run 2026-10-12. Price used: 88.44 US dollars (NYSE, live quote 2026-10-12).*

**Data caveat first.** The transcript block labelled 30 July 2026 in this run's file is a repeat of the 31 July 2025 call (fiscal fourth quarter 2025): the chief executive opens with "the fourth quarter of fiscal 25, ended 06/30/2025" and the same 856 million dollars of loan growth and 4.84% margin. The genuine fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter call (30 July 2026) is therefore not in the file. Fiscal 2026 results used below come from this committee's own prior verified record (company release of 30 July 2026, filed statements of 20 August 2026) and from the FMP earnings record (June-quarter 2026 earnings per share of 2.20 dollars against a 2.16 estimate).

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
Across the five calls from July 2025 to April 2026 the story moved from "best-in-class margin with or without the FDIC purchased-loan accretion" (July 2025) to "diversified loan growth plus acquired deposits and leases" (Verdant Commercial Capital closed 30 September 2025; about 2.3 billion dollars of Jenius Bank deposits converted around the end of April 2026). The margin claim was quietly re-anchored: as the discount accretion on the loan pool bought from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ran off, management leaned more on loan growth and fee businesses (adviser custody, clearing) and on an explicit expense discipline rule. Crypto and stablecoin interest surfaced in July 2025 ("we are focused on it and thinking through it") but has produced nothing concrete.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Book value per share compounds high-teens | 5-year book value per share growth +19.2% a year; 18% year on year in July 2025 | Corroborated |
| Earnings growth | Earnings per share 3.97 (FY22) to 8.48 (FY26), but 7.66 to 7.43 dip in FY25; FY26 +14% | Corroborated, lumpy |
| Best-in-class margin ex-accretion | Reported margin fell from 4.94% (Dec 2025 qtr) to 4.57% (Mar 2026 qtr) as accretion ran off | Holding, but cushion gone |
| Credit quality improving | Non-accrual loans fell from 1.26% to 0.61% of loans over five quarters | Corroborated |
| Compensation growth capped at 30% of revenue growth | Held through two acquisitions | Corroborated |
| Earnings quality | Pre-tax income fell 175.5m to 165.3m to 156.0m over the last three reported quarters while the tax rate fell 26.8% to 24.6% to 19.9% | Reported growth flattered by tax |

The story is slightly richer than the pre-tax trajectory: the last two reported quarters of earnings-per-share growth came from the tax line, part of which is linked to the share price via stock-compensation accounting and will not repeat at a lower price.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Stable to rising. The chief executive gives specific, falsifiable targets (the 30% compensation-to-revenue-growth rule, "that is a public goal that the team is gonna hit") and is blunt about credit ("a handful of stuff rattling around" in commercial and industrial loans, "nothing of any significant materiality"). Language remains offensive (new floor-plan lending team, tech-sector deposit team, middle-market team) rather than defensive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
High. Verdant integration came in ahead of plan, the Jenius conversion happened on the date given, the expense rule was met. The beat rate is 6 of 7 quarters (86%); the one miss was the March 2026 quarter (1.90 against 2.13), driven by acquisition and funding timing. One soft spot: management guided a 26-27% tax rate and has booked well below it without explaining how much is repeatable.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
Analysts ask about loan-category mix, deposit costs and credit, and get full answers. Nobody has asked about the share-price-linked tax benefit or how a bank funding about 85% of deposits with rate-paying accounts holds its margin while the Federal Reserve is raising rates (the 16 September 2026 increase was the first since July 2023). That is the unexamined question.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: pre-tax income down two straight quarters to June 2026, masked by the tax rate.
- Red: rate-paying deposit base in a hiking cycle; margin has lost its accretion cushion.
- Red: concentration in lending to non-bank financial firms and specialty commercial real estate while private-credit defaults run at records.
- Red: 5 open-market insider sales and no buys (latest input).
- Green: five consecutive quarters of falling non-accrual loans.
- Green: published, met expense rule; book value compounding; no dividend leakage.
- Green: diversified sticky commercial deposits via software and payment integrations (July 2025).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
"Best-in-class margin" has shifted from a headline number to an exclusion-based claim. The phrase "average bank stuff" about commercial and industrial lending (July 2025) is a quiet admission that newer loan categories will carry ordinary bank losses. Stablecoin remarks are deliberately non-committal.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: strengthening. The single thing to weigh before sizing: whether the net interest margin holds near 4.5% through the hiking cycle, first tested in the fiscal first-quarter 2027 results due 29 October 2026 (confirmed by the company on 29 September 2026). The moat is a narrow cost-advantage and scale moat from a branchless deposit platform plus sticky integrated commercial deposits; return on equity of about 16% is stable rather than falling. Fintech and stablecoin disintermediation is a manageable rather than terminal threat: the low multiple is a fair price for a rate-sensitive bank, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
thesis_evidence: The business case is corroborated by the latest dated numbers: fiscal 2026 (year to 30 June 2026, reported 30 July 2026, filed 20 August 2026) earnings per share of 8.48 dollars, up about 14 percent; June-quarter 2026 earnings per share of 2.20 against a 2.16 estimate (FMP earnings record); non-accrual loans down to 0.61 percent of loans; book value per share still compounding high-teens. The two soft spots - pre-tax income down two straight quarters masked by a falling tax rate, and margin pressure as purchased-loan accretion runs off - have been known since July 2026 and do not disprove the claim. The price drift from 91.25 dollars (22 September) to 88.44 dollars (12 October 2026) was a sector-wide, rate-driven drift with no company news.
macro_fit_note: The backdrop on 12 October 2026 reads reflation (growth and inflation both accelerating) in a debt-cycle phase where positive real long rates are being imposed and cash earned now is rewarded - Axos earns and retains about 16 percent on equity today, a plus - but a bank funding most deposits with rate-paying accounts carries funding-cost risk if rates keep rising, so the net is neutral over the 18-month horizon. Inflation resilience is not measurable from a bank's accounts; no pass-through evidence in the transcript.
entry_plain: buy near 82 USD, which a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off could deliver

bull_thesis: Axos is a branchless digital bank that earns like a top-decile lender and trades like an average one. Management reiterated low-to-mid-teens loan growth for fiscal 2027 and expects the large loans that slipped from September to close in December. About 75% of loans reprice within 30 days, so a higher-for-longer rate path, with a December Fed hike about 85% priced, supports the margin. High-yield spreads are widening into this window (CCC-rated debt about 1,100bp over BB on 2026-10-30, HY +30bp in two sessions). Axos has just taken its first realized losses in its syndicated cash-flow loan book: two charge-offs in the September 2026 quarter, one a healthcare borrower hit by regulation and one hurt by tariffs, both led by non-bank agents. consensus_delta: The street's view is broadly correct but slightly too optimistic on timing.
